newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh SEC head quits, alleges lack of support.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh SEC head quits, alleges lack of support.

text.p: The head of Bangladesh's Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Harunur Rashid, said he had resigned in protest at a lack of cooperation and support from the government in his efforts to revamp the troubled capital market.

"I decided to resign because I had not been getting cooperation from the relevant authorities. If I am not able to contribute to the development of the capital market, (then) why should I be holding my post?" said Rashid, chairman of the SEC, the capital market watchdog.
Rashid said he had submitted the letter of resignation to the government on June 29, after serving as SEC chief for about 11 months, but was still awaiting a reply.

"We have received his resignation letter. We are examining his complaints. The fate of the letter (whether it will be accepted) has yet to be decided," one finance ministry official told Reuters on Wednesday.
"The final decision will come from the Prime Minister."

Rashid said he felt frustrated as the authorities, including the finance ministry, did not support his reform plans after the country's main Dhaka Stock Exchange (DSE) was rocked by unusual fluctuations in share prices.
The DSE index shot up to 3,700 points in November 1996 before nose-diving to about 1,200 in March and has since been hovering at around 1,100.
In his resignation letter, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters, Rashid detailed the reasons for his decision.
"Certain interferences in the activities of the SEC by the finance ministry...undermined the effectiveness of the SEC and adversely affected it's activities," Rashid alleged.

The government appointed an inquiry committee headed by Amirul Islam Chowdhury, Vice-Chancellor of Jahangirnagar University, in 1996. A preliminary report by the committee implicated 15 top brokers and company owners in manipulating share prices. The accused are facing legal proceedings.
The committee recommended immediate computerisation of DSE trading and increased manpower for the SEC, but both proposals have yet to be implemented, SEC officials said.
They said the SEC now had only 11 officials.

Susan Selwyn, a consultant of the World Bank, said in a report that "the SEC has been coping well in the crisis considering that it is newly established (in 1993), (and) is under-staffed by at least 400 percent on a conservative estimate."
"The SEC must increase its establishment of staff and be offered extensive training programmes... The SEC is constrained from carrying out its legal duties for fear of political backlash."
